concept: ma masdariyya is forced when the following verb carries no resumptive pronoun that could refer back to ma
prompt: In عَجِبْتُ مِمَّا صَنَعْتَ ("I was amazed at what you made"), the verb صَنَعْتَ carries no resumptive pronoun that could refer back to مَا (compare عَجِبْتُ مِمَّا صَنَعْتَهُ, which does have one). A learner used to the more frequent relative reading of مَا insists this مَا is still موصولة ("that which") because a relative reading is the pattern they meet most often. Evaluate the claim using the resumptive-pronoun test and state مَا's actual function here.
expected_answer: The claim is wrong. Relative ma needs a resumptive pronoun somewhere in its clause referring back to it, and صَنَعْتَ carries none, so a relative reading is structurally unavailable here regardless of how frequent it is elsewhere. Because the following verb has no resumptive pronoun, ma can only be ma masdariyya: it converts صَنَعْتَ into the equivalent of a verbal noun, so the phrase paraphrases as min sun'ika, "from your making it". A structural restriction from the clause itself overrides frequency.
accepted_variants: Wrong: with no resumptive pronoun on صَنَعْتَ, the relative reading is structurally blocked, so ma here is ma masdariyya, equivalent to min sun'ika, not the relative 'that which'.
forbidden_answers: The claim is correct: ma here is the relative meaning 'that which', since ma almost always introduces a relative clause and the frequent reading should be trusted over a structural detail like a missing pronoun.
required_reasoning: relative ma requires a resumptive pronoun referring back to it
the following verb carries no resumptive pronoun
with no resumptive pronoun the reading must be ma masdariyya, not relative
the phrase paraphrases as a verbal noun, min sun'ika
explanation: Frequency of a reading elsewhere is not evidence for a given occurrence: the resumptive-pronoun test is the structural signal that decides relative-vs-masdariyya ma here, and it must be checked before defaulting to the commoner reading.

concept: ba'da and qabla fused with ma categorically select ma masdariyya zarfiyya, closing off the relative reading before the following clause is even read
prompt: بَعْدَ and قَبْلَ fuse with مَا into the fixed compounds بَعْدَمَا and قَبْلَمَا, which are always temporal ma masdariyya and never accept the relative reading, whatever the following clause looks like. In انْتَظَرْتُ بَعْدَمَا خَرَجْتَ ("I waited after you left"), a learner reasons that because خَرَجْتَ could in principle be read with a resumptive pronoun elsewhere, this clause should be parsed as a relative clause "after that which you left". Evaluate this reasoning and state what actually fixes ma's function here.
expected_answer: The reasoning is wrong. بَعْدَ and قَبْلَ fused with مَا categorically select temporal ma masdariyya; this is a closed restriction imposed by the preceding particle itself, not a property decided clause-by-clause from the following verb. So the phrase can only mean "after your leaving", never "after that which you left"; the category of the preceding particle overrides any relative possibility before the following clause is even examined.
accepted_variants: Wrong: ba'da/qabla fused with ma categorically force temporal ma masdariyya, so the phrase can only mean 'after your leaving', never a relative clause, regardless of the following verb.
forbidden_answers: The reasoning is correct: since a relative reading is possible whenever a verb like خَرَجْتَ appears, the phrase should be read as 'after that which you left'.
required_reasoning: ba'da and qabla fused with ma categorically select temporal ma masdariyya
this restriction is imposed by the preceding particle, not decided from the following verb
the phrase means 'after your leaving', never a relative clause
explanation: A category restriction imposed by the immediately preceding particle is a hard constraint that must be checked first, before any property of the following clause is allowed to suggest a rival reading.

concept: ma masdariyya is mabni with no visible case; as the second term of a construct its masdar-equivalent clause occupies only the position of the genitive
prompt: In أَعْجَبَنِي حُسْنُ مَا فَعَلْتَ ("the goodness of what you did impressed me"), حُسْنُ is the first term of an annexation and مَا فَعَلْتَ is its second term. Because فَعَلْتَ carries no resumptive pronoun, ma here is ma masdariyya, standing for the masdar fi'lika. A learner marks the whole ma-clause with a nominative ending, reasoning that the second term of a construct should agree with common noun endings they have seen. Evaluate this and state the correct case treatment of the second term.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. Ma masdariyya is mabni (indeclinable): it carries no visible case ending of its own, not a nominative one. As the second term of the annexation, its masdar-equivalent clause sits in the position of the genitive, the same slot fi'lika would occupy if the masdar were written out directly, but the visible ending on ma itself is absent, not nominative.
accepted_variants: Wrong: ma masdariyya is mabni and carries no visible ending; the second-term clause occupies the position of the genitive, but there is no nominative mark to assign.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: since the second term of a construct can carry its own ending like any noun, the ma-clause should be marked nominative in agreement with common construct patterns.
required_reasoning: ma masdariyya is mabni and carries no visible case ending
the masdar-equivalent clause occupies the position of the genitive as the construct's second term
there is no nominative ending to assign to a mabni element
explanation: A construct's second term takes the genitive, but when that term is a mabni masdariyya-ma clause, the genitive is positional, never a visible ending copied from ordinary declinable nouns.

concept: a resumptive pronoun marks ma relative, and a relative-clause subject makes the whole sentence nominal, not verbal, before any case is assigned
prompt: In مَا فَعَلْتَهُ صَوَابٌ ("what you did is correct"), فَعَلْتَهُ carries the resumptive pronoun -hu referring back to ma, so the whole مَا فَعَلْتَهُ is a relative noun clause functioning as the subject of a nominal sentence, with صَوَابٌ as its predicate. A learner opens by classifying the sentence as verbal because it starts with what looks like a verb-adjacent particle, and then struggles to place صَوَابٌ. Evaluate the learner's opening classification and state the correct sentence type and role of ma.
expected_answer: The learner's opening classification is wrong. Because فَعَلْتَهُ carries a resumptive pronoun referring back to ma, ma here is relative, and the relative clause as a whole is a nominal, not a verbal, sentence: ma is the subject and صَوَابٌ is its predicate. The sentence type must be identified from this relative-clause-as-subject structure before any case or role is assigned, not from the surface impression that a verb opens the sentence.
accepted_variants: Wrong: the resumptive pronoun marks ma as relative, and the whole relative clause is a nominal sentence with ma as the subject and صَوَابٌ as the predicate, not a verbal sentence.
forbidden_answers: The learner's classification is correct: since the sentence opens with ma plus a verb, it should be treated as a verbal sentence with صَوَابٌ left unplaced.
required_reasoning: the resumptive pronoun on فَعَلْتَهُ marks ma as relative
the relative clause functions as the subject of a nominal sentence
ma is the subject and صَوَابٌ is the predicate
explanation: A relative ma-clause heading a sentence makes that sentence nominal, with the whole relative clause as its subject; the sentence type must be read from that structure, not guessed from the first written word.

concept: endings follow the parsed role of a gap-relative ma clause; vocalising word by word in reading order before parsing risks an unlicensed ending
prompt: In مَا صَنَعْتَ حَسَنٌ ("what you made is good"), صَنَعْتَ is transitive with no separate object and no resumptive pronoun; ma itself fills the missing object slot, and the whole ma-clause is the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is حَسَنٌ. A learner starts by placing endings on each word in reading order before deciding what ma itself is doing. Evaluate this approach and state what must be settled first.
expected_answer: The approach is backwards. Endings are consequences of grammatical role, and the role of ma here -- a gap-relative filling the verb's missing object, heading a nominal clause that is itself the subject, with حَسَنٌ as the predicate -- can only be read after the sentence's structure is parsed, not before. Vocalising word by word in reading order, before recognising that the ma-clause as a whole is the subject and حَسَنٌ its predicate, risks assigning an ending the parse does not license.
accepted_variants: Wrong to vocalise first: ma is the gap-relative object of صَنَعْتَ, and the whole ma-clause is the subject with حَسَنٌ as predicate; the parse must be settled before any ending is assigned.
forbidden_answers: The approach is fine: since Arabic words each carry their own default ending, it is safe to vocalise the verb and the predicate in reading order and only afterward consider what ma is doing.
required_reasoning: the verb has no separate object and no resumptive pronoun, so ma fills its missing object slot
the ma-clause as a whole is the subject of a nominal sentence
حَسَنٌ is the predicate
endings follow the parse and cannot be assigned before it
explanation: Most Arabic endings are determined by grammatical role, which is only available once the sentence's structure -- here, a gap-relative ma heading the subject clause -- has been parsed; vocalising in surface reading order before that risks an unlicensed ending.

concept: an intervening illa breaks ma hijaziyya's laysa-like negation into a restriction, cancelling its government so both ism and khabar stay nominative
prompt: ما can act like لَيْسَ (ism marfu', khabar mansub) only under conditions; one of those conditions is that the negation must not be broken by إلا. In مَا زَيْدٌ إِلَّا قَائِمٌ ("Zayd is only standing"), a learner keeps قَائِمٌ accusative (قَائِمًا), reasoning that ما still governs the predicate the way it does in a plain مَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا sentence. Evaluate this and state the correct case of the predicate here.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. Once إلا intervenes and turns the sentence into a restriction ("only standing"), ما's laysa-like government is cancelled entirely: both the subject and the predicate revert to ordinary nominal-sentence agreement and stay nominative, so it must be قَائِمٌ, not قَائِمًا. The government that would apply in a plain negation without إلا does not survive the restriction.
accepted_variants: Wrong: إلا breaking the negation into a restriction cancels ma's laysa-like government, so the predicate stays nominative (قَائِمٌ), not accusative.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: ma always governs its predicate into the accusative regardless of what follows, so قَائِمًا is correct even with إلا present.
required_reasoning: إلا breaks the negation into a restriction
this cancels ma's laysa-like government entirely
both subject and predicate revert to ordinary nominative agreement
explanation: Ma's government is conditional, not automatic: an intervening إلا is one of the named conditions that cancels it, and dropping case agreement on the predicate after that trigger is exactly the error the condition exists to catch.

concept: fronting the predicate before the subject cancels ma hijaziyya's government, leaving both terms nominative
prompt: Another condition on ma's laysa-like government is that the predicate must not precede the subject. In مَا قَائِمٌ زَيْدٌ (predicate قَائِمٌ fronted before the subject زَيْدٌ, "Zayd is not standing"), a learner supplies only the fronted predicate and marks it accusative (قَائِمًا), as if the normal مَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا government still applied despite the reordering. Evaluate this and state the correct case of both terms.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. Fronting the predicate before the subject is itself one of the named conditions that cancels ma's laysa-like government, so the construction cannot supply only a governed accusative predicate: once fronted, both the predicate and the subject revert to plain nominative agreement, giving قَائِمٌ زَيْدٌ, not قَائِمًا زَيْدٌ.
accepted_variants: Wrong: fronting the predicate before the subject cancels ma's government, so both terms are nominative (قَائِمٌ زَيْدٌ), not an accusative predicate.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: word order does not affect ma's government, so the fronted predicate should still be marked accusative as قَائِمًا.
required_reasoning: fronting the predicate before the subject is a named condition that cancels ma's government
once fronted, both terms revert to nominative agreement
the predicate cannot be supplied alone still marked accusative
explanation: Ma's laysa-like government depends on the subject keeping its normal position before the predicate; reordering is not a cosmetic detail, it is one of the triggers that switches off the government altogether.

concept: fronting a complement of the khabar before the subject also cancels ma hijaziyya's government over the khabar itself, even though that complement keeps its own case
prompt: A further condition on ma's government: if a complement belonging to the predicate is fronted before the subject, the government over the predicate itself is cancelled, even though the fronted complement keeps its own case. In مَا طَعَامَكَ زَيْدٌ آكِلٌ ("Zayd is not eating your food"; طَعَامَكَ is the object of the predicate آكِلٌ, fronted before the subject زَيْدٌ), a learner reads this the same as a bare clause negation and marks آكِلٌ accusative (آكِلًا), treating the fronting as irrelevant to the predicate's own case. Evaluate this and state the correct case of آكِلٌ.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. Fronting طَعَامَكَ (the predicate's own complement) before the subject زَيْدٌ is itself a trigger that cancels ma's government over the predicate آكِلٌ, so آكِلٌ must be nominative, not accusative; طَعَامَكَ itself keeps its own accusative case as the object of آكِلٌ regardless, since that case comes from آكِلٌ's own verbal-noun government, not from ما.
accepted_variants: Wrong: fronting the predicate's own complement before the subject cancels ma's government over the predicate, so آكِلٌ stays nominative even though طَعَامَكَ itself keeps its own accusative case.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: since ما always negates the whole clause the same way, آكِلًا should stay accusative no matter what is fronted before the subject.
required_reasoning: fronting the predicate's own complement before the subject cancels ma's government over the predicate
the predicate itself must therefore be nominative
the fronted complement keeps its own case independently of ma
explanation: Two different case assignments are at work here: the fronted complement's own accusative case (from the predicate's verbal-noun government) survives, while ma's government over the predicate itself is cancelled by the very act of fronting that complement.

concept: bal after ma hijaziyya opens a fresh, independently-cased correction rather than continuing the original accusative government
prompt: After بَل ("rather", correcting/upgrading the first claim), the corrected term is understood as a fresh nominal predication of its own, not a continuation of ما's original government. In مَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا بَلْ قَاعِدٌ ("Zayd is not standing, but rather sitting"), a learner marks قَاعِدٌ accusative (قَاعِدًا), reasoning that بَلْ is just a plain contrastive connective like a comma and the original government over قَائِمًا should carry straight through to the corrected term. Evaluate this and state the correct case of the corrected term.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. بَلْ does not merely continue the sentence; it introduces a correction understood as its own resumed nominal predication (as if "بل هو قاعدٌ"), independent of ما's original accusative government over قَائِمًا. The corrected term therefore takes its own nominative case, قَاعِدٌ, not the accusative that governed the term بَلْ is correcting.
accepted_variants: Wrong: bal introduces a fresh, independently-cased correction, so the corrected term is nominative (قَاعِدٌ), not a continuation of ma's accusative government.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: bal is a plain contrastive connective, so the original accusative government over قَائِمًا carries straight through to قَاعِدًا.
required_reasoning: bal introduces a correction understood as its own resumed nominal predication
this is independent of ma's original government over the term being corrected
the corrected term takes its own nominative case
explanation: A corrective بَل does not extend the original government past itself; treating it as a plain contrastive connective wrongly assumes the corrected term inherits a case it was never assigned.

concept: a preceding interrogative hamza converts ma away from laysa-like negation entirely into a rhetorical question with no case government at all
prompt: When an interrogative hamza is prefixed to ما (أَمَا), the resulting particle is read as a rhetorical confirming question ("isn't it that...?", implying the affirmative), and ما no longer functions as the laysa-like negator at all. In أَمَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ؟ ("isn't Zayd standing?", implying he certainly is), a learner still applies ما's laysa-like government and marks the predicate accusative (قَائِمًا), treating the interrogative hamza as a cosmetic addition to an ordinary negated sentence. Evaluate this and state the correct case of the predicate.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. Prefixing the interrogative hamza converts أَمَا into a rhetorical question particle, not a negator at all, so ما's laysa-like government never applies here in the first place: the sentence is an ordinary nominal sentence (subject + predicate, both nominative) read as a rhetorical question, giving قَائِمٌ, not قَائِمًا.
accepted_variants: Wrong: the interrogative hamza converts the whole particle into a rhetorical question marker, not a negator, so ma's laysa-like government never applies and the predicate stays nominative, قَائِمٌ.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: the interrogative hamza is only decorative, so ما still negates the sentence with its usual government and the predicate should be accusative, قَائِمًا.
required_reasoning: prefixing the interrogative hamza converts the particle into a rhetorical question marker, not a negator
ma's laysa-like government therefore never applies
the sentence is an ordinary nominal sentence with both terms nominative
explanation: An interrogative hamza prefixed to ما does not merely decorate a negated sentence; it removes the negation reading altogether, so the case-government question must be re-asked from the rhetorical-question structure, not from the laysa-like frame.

concept: amma is a1n fused with ma kaffa, presupposing an unstated general condition, and is not ordinary coordination
prompt: أَمَّا is historically إِنْ (the conditional particle) fused with a preventive مَا that neutralizes إِنْ's own government, together presupposing an unstated general antecedent ("whatever the case may be"). In أَمَّا زَيْدٌ فَقَائِمٌ ("as for Zayd, he is standing"), a learner treats أَمَّا as a plain coordinator, expecting a second coordinand to follow فَ the way وَ would expect one. Evaluate this and state what أَمَّا actually presupposes and what فَ is doing here.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. أَمَّا is not a coordinator; it is a fossilized conditional-like particle (إِنْ fused with a preventive مَا) presupposing an unstated general condition ("whatever the case may be, as for Zayd..."). The فَ that follows is not linking two coordinands; it is the obligatory jawab-fa introducing this particle's apodosis, here the predicate قَائِمٌ about زَيْدٌ.
accepted_variants: Wrong: amma presupposes an unstated general condition and is not a coordinator; the following fa is the obligatory jawab-fa of that conditional-like frame, not a link to a second coordinand.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: amma is an ordinary coordinating particle like wa, and the fa is simply linking زيد to قائم as two coordinands.
required_reasoning: amma is a conditional particle fused with a preventive ma, not a coordinator
it presupposes an unstated general condition
the following fa is the obligatory jawab-fa of that frame, introducing the predicate about زيد
explanation: Reading amma as ordinary coordination misses that it is a fossilized conditional frame with its own presupposed antecedent; the fa that follows belongs to that frame's apodosis, not to a coordination structure.

concept: the jawab-fa after amma is obligatory precisely because a nominal predicate cannot attach directly to the neutralized conditional particle
prompt: Because أَمَّا is a conditional-like particle whose own government has been neutralized by the fused preventive مَا, its apodosis cannot attach directly the way an ordinary sentence would; the جواب needs the linking فَ, especially when the apodosis is a bare nominal predicate. A learner writes أَمَّا زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ, omitting the فَ before the predicate, reasoning that since قَائِمٌ is just an ordinary nominal predicate it needs no special linking device. Evaluate this and state why the sentence is ungrammatical as written.
expected_answer: The sentence is ungrammatical. Even though قَائِمٌ is an ordinary nominal predicate in isolation, أَمَّا's own government has been neutralized, so its apodosis cannot attach to it directly the way a plain subject attaches to a plain predicate; the جواب-فَ is obligatory here precisely because there is no other link available. The sentence must be أَمَّا زَيْدٌ فَقَائِمٌ.
accepted_variants: Ungrammatical as written: amma's neutralized government means its apodosis cannot attach directly, so the jawab-fa is obligatory even before an ordinary nominal predicate; it must be أَمَّا زَيْدٌ فَقَائِمٌ.
forbidden_answers: The sentence is fine as written: since قَائِمٌ is an ordinary nominal predicate, it needs no linking fa and أَمَّا زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ is a complete correct sentence.
required_reasoning: amma's own government is neutralized by the fused preventive ma
its apodosis therefore cannot attach directly to it
the jawab-fa is obligatory even before an ordinary nominal predicate
explanation: An ordinary nominal predicate needing no linking device is true of a plain subject-predicate pair, but amma is not a plain subject; its neutralized government is exactly why the jawab-fa cannot be treated as optional.

concept: the jawab-fa after amma is likewise obligatory before a future-marked or imperative apodosis, which cannot attach to amma directly either
prompt: أَمَّا's جواب-فَ is equally required when the apodosis opens with a future-marked verb (سَـ / سَوْفَ) or an imperative, both of which likewise cannot attach directly to the neutralized particle. A learner writes أَمَّا أَنْتَ سَتَنْجَحُ, omitting فَ before the future-marked verb, on the reasoning that a future-marked verb is still just an ordinary verbal predicate. Evaluate this and state the correct form.
expected_answer: The sentence is ungrammatical as written. A future-marked (or imperative) apodosis is exactly the kind of clause that cannot attach directly to amma's neutralized government, so the jawab-fa remains obligatory here too; the sentence must be أَمَّا أَنْتَ فَسَتَنْجَحُ, with فَ introducing the future-marked apodosis.
accepted_variants: Ungrammatical as written: a future-marked apodosis still cannot attach directly to amma, so the jawab-fa is obligatory; it must be أَمَّا أَنْتَ فَسَتَنْجَحُ.
forbidden_answers: The sentence is fine as written: a future-marked verb is an ordinary verbal predicate that needs no linking fa, so أَمَّا أَنْتَ سَتَنْجَحُ is complete and correct.
required_reasoning: a future-marked or imperative apodosis cannot attach directly to amma's neutralized government
the jawab-fa remains obligatory in this case as well
the correct form places fa before the future-marked verb
explanation: The obligatory jawab-fa is not limited to nominal predicates; any apodosis type that cannot attach directly to amma's neutralized government, including a future-marked or imperative clause, still needs it.

concept: the jawab-fa after amma carries a structurally required resultative link, not the loose plain-addition sense of an ordinary coordinating wa
prompt: A learner treats the فَ after أَمَّا as interchangeable with the plain coordinating وَ, reasoning that both simply mean "and" in English translation, and so freely swaps أَمَّا زَيْدٌ فَقَائِمٌ for a version using وَ instead of فَ. Evaluate this substitution and state what the جواب-فَ specifically contributes that a plain وَ does not.
expected_answer: The substitution is wrong. The فَ after أَمَّا is not an ordinary coordinator; it is the obligatory jawab-fa completing amma's neutralized conditional-like frame, linking the topic to its predicate as a structurally required apodosis-link. A plain وَ only asserts addition between two independent items and cannot fill this obligatory linking role; swapping it in leaves amma's apodosis without its required attachment.
accepted_variants: Wrong: the fa after amma is the obligatory jawab-fa completing its conditional-like frame, not a plain coordinating wa, and wa cannot fill that obligatory linking role.
forbidden_answers: The substitution is fine: fa and wa both just mean 'and', so either one can introduce the predicate after amma without changing the sentence's grammar.
required_reasoning: the fa after amma is the obligatory jawab-fa of its conditional-like frame, not an ordinary coordinator
a plain wa only asserts addition between independent items
wa cannot fill the obligatory apodosis-linking role that amma's frame requires
explanation: Two particles that both translate loosely as 'and' can still have entirely different grammatical jobs; amma's fa is load-bearing structurally in a way a plain coordinating wa never is.

concept: the jawab-fa after amma must appear even where an English rendering would use no linking word at all
prompt: Because English often renders أَمَّا ... فَـ with no separate linking word ("as for Zayd, standing"), a learner drops the فَ from the Arabic itself in a terse apodosis, writing أَمَّا زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ and reasoning that since the English translation needs no linking word, the Arabic does not either. Evaluate this reasoning and state what the English rendering does and does not tell you about the Arabic.
expected_answer: The reasoning is wrong. The English translation's own economy says nothing about the Arabic particle's own requirement: أَمَّا's neutralized government still needs the جواب-فَ to attach its apodosis, in any apodosis shape, however short. The English gloss simply does not need a separate word for a job Arabic marks morphologically with فَ, so أَمَّا زَيْدٌ فَقَائِمٌ keeps the فَ even though a terse English rendering may drop an equivalent word.
accepted_variants: Wrong: the English translation's economy does not license dropping the Arabic fa; amma's own neutralized government still requires the jawab-fa regardless of how the English is phrased.
forbidden_answers: The reasoning is correct: since the natural English translation needs no linking word here, the Arabic fa is optional and may be safely dropped in a short apodosis.
required_reasoning: the English translation's economy does not reflect the Arabic particle's own requirement
amma's neutralized government still requires the jawab-fa in any apodosis shape
the fa must not be dropped even in a terse apodosis
explanation: A translation-driven omission conflates what English needs to say with what Arabic morphology needs to mark; amma's jawab-fa is a grammatical requirement of the Arabic frame, not a stylistic linking word that a translation can license dropping.

concept: the answer-expectation test -- does the utterance expect an answer, or express astonishment with none expected -- must run before any case is assigned, since exclamatory ma and interrogative ma license entirely different case patterns on the same skeleton
prompt: مَا أَجْمَلَ السَّمَاءَ! (exclamatory: "how beautiful the sky is!", no answer expected, أَجْمَلَ is a frozen taʿajjub verb whose object السَّمَاءَ is accusative) and مَا أَجْمَلُ الأَشْيَاءِ عِنْدَكَ؟ (interrogative: "what is the most beautiful thing you have?", an answer is expected, أَجْمَلُ is an ordinary elative predicate annexed to a genitive) share the same skeleton أجمل. A learner assigns case to السَّمَاءَ/الأَشْيَاءِ from the skeleton alone, without first running the answer-expectation test. Evaluate this approach and state what the test decides.
expected_answer: The approach is wrong. The same skeleton أجمل licenses two structurally different constructions with two different case patterns, and only the answer-expectation test (does the utterance expect an answer, or express astonishment with none expected) decides which is meant: no answer expected selects the frozen exclamatory verb with an accusative object, while an expected answer selects the ordinary elative predicate with a genitive annexed complement. Case cannot be assigned from the bare skeleton before that test is run.

concept: ma dama is not negation, so its kana-sister khabar is an ordinary declinable accusative noun that keeps its full nunation, unlike the mabni bare noun after the categorical negator la
prompt: اجْتَهِدْ مَا دُمْتَ حَيًّا ("strive as long as you are alive") uses the durative kana-sister دَامَ, whose khabar حَيًّا is an ordinary declinable accusative noun. A learner, misreading ما دام as a form of categorical negation resembling لا النافية للجنس, drops the tanween from حَيًّا, writing it as a bare fixed form with no nunation, the treatment that applies only to a bare noun negated by لا. Evaluate this and state the correct treatment of حَيًّا.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. This ما is not negation at all; ما دام is a fossilized temporal-masdariyya frame ("as long as ... lasts"), and دُمْتَ is an ordinary kana-sister verb whose khabar is حَيًّا, a normal declinable accusative noun. It keeps its full tanween exactly like any other indefinite accusative noun; the bare-fatha-with-no-nunation treatment belongs only to the negated noun after the categorical negator la, an entirely unrelated construction that this negation-resembling surface of ma has nothing to do with here.
accepted_variants: Wrong: ma dama is not negation, so حَيًّا is an ordinary declinable accusative noun keeping its full tanween; the no-nunation bare-fatha treatment belongs only to la al-nafiya's own negated noun.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: since ma dama superficially resembles categorical negation, حَيًّا should be treated as a bare fixed form with no nunation, the same way la's negated noun is.
required_reasoning: ma dama is not negation, it is a fossilized temporal-masdariyya frame
دام is an ordinary kana-sister verb whose khabar is a normal declinable accusative noun
the no-nunation bare-fatha treatment belongs only to la al-nafiya's negated noun
explanation: A surface resemblance to a negation particle does not make a construction negation; ma dama's own khabar follows ordinary declension rules, and importing an unrelated negated-noun treatment onto it is a category error.

concept: ma dama is a fixed frame using the perfect verb dama, with no jussive-governing negation at all, so no mood question analogous to a prohibition ever arises inside it
prompt: اجْلِسْ مَا دَامَ الجَوُّ جَمِيلًا ("sit as long as the weather is beautiful") fixes دَامَ in the perfect tense inside the ما دام frame. A learner, primed by ما's superficial resemblance to a prohibitive/negative particle like لا الناهية, wrongly conjugates the verb inside ما دام into a jussive-looking present form, writing مَا يَدُمِ الجَوُّ جَمِيلًا, as though ما here governed a mood the way a prohibition would. Evaluate this and state the correct, fixed form.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. ما دام is a fixed durative-limit frame that uses the perfect verb دَامَ; it does not involve a jussive-governing negator at all, so there is no mood question to resolve the way there would be under لا الناهية. The correct, fixed form keeps the perfect: مَا دَامَ الجَوُّ جَمِيلًا, not a jussive-looking مَا يَدُمِ الجَوُّ. Reading a statement of duration as if it carried a prohibition's mood exponent confuses two entirely different ما-bearing constructions.
accepted_variants: Wrong: ma dama is a fixed frame using the perfect verb دام with no jussive-governing negator involved at all, so the correct form stays مَا دَامَ الجَوُّ جَمِيلًا, not a jussive-looking form.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: since ما can govern a prohibition elsewhere, ما دام should likewise put the verb in a jussive-looking present form, مَا يَدُمِ الجَوُّ جَمِيلًا.
required_reasoning: ma dama is a fixed frame using the perfect verb دام
it does not involve a jussive-governing negator
there is no mood question analogous to a prohibition inside this frame
explanation: Ma's ability to combine with jussive government elsewhere (as in la al-nahiya) does not transfer to the fixed ma-dama frame, which keeps the perfect verb and raises no mood question at all.

concept: ma inside the fixed ma-dama frame contributes no negation at all, and reading it as negation reverses the sentence's entire sense
prompt: سَأُسَاعِدُكَ مَا دُمْتَ صَادِقًا ("I will help you as long as you are truthful") uses the fixed durative frame ما دام. A learner, seeing the familiar negator shape مَا, reads the clause as negated, taking it to mean something like "I will help you as long as you are not truthful" (or that the whole clause denies the addressee's truthfulness). Evaluate this reading and state what ما actually contributes here.
expected_answer: The learner's reading reverses the sentence's sense. Despite looking identical to the negator ما, the ما inside the fixed ما دام frame contributes no negation whatsoever; ما دام together is a durative time-limit connective meaning "as long as / for as long as ... lasts". So the sentence means "I will help you for as long as you are truthful", asserting the addressee's truthfulness as the condition for help, not denying it; reading ما as negation here inverts the entire meaning of the frame.
accepted_variants: Wrong, the reading is reversed: ma inside ma-dama contributes no negation at all; the frame means 'as long as ... lasts', so the sentence asserts the addressee's truthfulness, not denies it.
forbidden_answers: The reading is correct: since ما is a negator, ما دام negates the following predicate, so the sentence means help is conditioned on the addressee NOT being truthful.
required_reasoning: ma inside the fixed ma-dama frame contributes no negation at all
ma dama together is a durative time-limit connective meaning 'as long as ... lasts'
reading ma as negation here reverses the sentence's actual meaning
explanation: A written particle's most common function elsewhere is not evidence for its function inside a fixed idiom; ma-dama is exactly the kind of frame where the component ma has been bleached of its ordinary negating force.

concept: ma al-nafiya never carries prohibitive force and never governs the jussive; a jussive ending after ma does not correspond to any real reading of ma at all
prompt: Compare مَا (statement negator, no mood effect, keeps the indicative) with لَا (which can be prohibitive, governing the jussive: لَا تَذْهَبْ, "do not go!"). Presented with the written form مَا تَذْهَبْ (jussive ending), a learner cannot decide whether this is a plain negative statement ("you do not go") marked with a stray jussive, or a legitimate prohibitive use of مَا ("do not go!"). Evaluate both readings and state which, if either, the jussive form licenses.
expected_answer: Neither reading licenses the jussive as written. مَا النافية never carries prohibitive force and never governs the following مضارع into the jussive; it simply negates a statement, and a statement negated by مَا keeps the indicative: مَا تَذْهَبُ ("you do not go"). Prohibition ("do not go!") is لَا's job (لَا تَذْهَبْ), not مَا's; the jussive form مَا تَذْهَبْ does not correspond to a real reading of مَا at all, and should not be read as either a plain statement or a legitimate prohibitive.
accepted_variants: Neither: ma al-nafiya never carries prohibitive force and never governs the jussive, so ما تذهب with a jussive ending is not a real reading of ma at all; the plain statement is مَا تَذْهَبُ, indicative.
forbidden_answers: The jussive form is a legitimate prohibitive use of ma, equivalent in force to لا تذهب, 'do not go!'.
required_reasoning: ma al-nafiya never carries prohibitive force
ma never governs the following mudari' into the jussive
a statement negated by ma keeps the indicative
prohibition is la's function, marked la ta-fal with the jussive
explanation: Mixing up which particle in a shared negation-family carries mood government is the exact error this misconception targets: ma's job is plain statement-negation, never prohibition, and it never touches the following verb's mood.

concept: only a mood-governing operator may change a verb's ending; ma is not one, so a verb negated by ma keeps the indicative
prompt: هُوَ مَا يَفْهَمُ الدَّرْسَ ("he does not understand the lesson") negates an ordinary present-tense statement. A learner writes هُوَ مَا يَفْهَمِ الدَّرْسَ, putting the verb in the jussive, reasoning that a negating particle should change the verb's ending the way لَمْ does. Evaluate this and state the correct ending and why.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. Only an operator that specifically governs mood -- such as لَمْ, or لَا in its prohibitive use -- may change the verb's ending; plain مَا has no mood effect at all, so the verb it negates keeps its own indicative ending regardless of the negation. The correct form is هُوَ مَا يَفْهَمُ الدَّرْسَ, not the jussive-marked يَفْهَمِ.
accepted_variants: Wrong: only a mood-governing operator like lam may change the verb's ending; plain ma has no mood effect, so the verb stays indicative, يَفْهَمُ, not the jussive يَفْهَمِ.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: since ma is a negating particle like lam, it should likewise change the verb's ending to the jussive, يَفْهَمِ.
required_reasoning: only an operator that specifically governs mood may change a verb's ending
plain ma has no mood effect at all
the correct ending here stays indicative, يَفْهَمُ
explanation: Sharing the general function of negation with lam does not give ma lam's mood-governing power; a mood change requires a specific mood-governing operator, and ma is not one.

concept: the negator must be chosen by the intended time reference, not by familiarity; lam specifically shifts a present-form verb to past meaning, so it cannot substitute for present-time negation
prompt: A learner wants to say "he does not understand the lesson" (present-time negation) but, out of familiarity with لَمْ from earlier lessons, writes هُوَ لَمْ يَفْهَمِ الدَّرْسَ. Evaluate this choice and state what it actually means, and what the learner should have written instead.
expected_answer: The choice is wrong for the intended meaning. لَمْ specifically shifts a present-form verb's reference to past time under its jussive government, so هُوَ لَمْ يَفْهَمِ الدَّرْسَ means "he did not understand the lesson" (a completed past failure to understand), not the intended present-time "he does not understand the lesson". For present-time negation, the correct choice is plain مَا with the indicative: هُوَ مَا يَفْهَمُ الدَّرْسَ.
accepted_variants: Wrong for the intended meaning: lam shifts reference to past time ('did not understand'); for present-time negation the correct choice is plain ma with the indicative, هُوَ مَا يَفْهَمُ الدَّرْسَ.
forbidden_answers: The choice is correct: lam is simply the standard way to negate any verb, present or past, so هُوَ لَمْ يَفْهَمِ الدَّرْسَ correctly expresses present-time negation.
required_reasoning: lam specifically shifts a present-form verb's reference to past time
the sentence as written means a completed past failure to understand, not present-time negation
present-time negation calls for plain ma with the indicative instead
explanation: Choosing a negator by familiarity rather than by the time reference it actually licenses produces a grammatical sentence with the wrong meaning; lam and ma are not interchangeable defaults for negation.

concept: ma al-istifhamiyya drops its alif when a preposition governs it directly; keeping the alif in that position signals a different function of ma, not the interrogative
prompt: لِمَ فَعَلْتَ ذَلِكَ؟ ("why did you do that?") fuses لِ with the interrogative مَا, which drops its alif under this direct government. A learner writes لِمَا فَعَلْتَ ذَلِكَ؟, keeping the alif, intending the same interrogative "why" meaning. Evaluate this and state what the written form actually signals and what the correct interrogative form is.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong to keep the alif. When مَا الاستفهامية is directly governed by a preposition, it drops its alif; لِ plus interrogative مَا is written لِمَ, not لِمَا. The written form لِمَا فَعَلْتَ ذَلِكَ still exists in Arabic, but it signals a different function of مَا (relative or masdariyya, roughly "because of that which you did"), not the interrogative "why". For the interrogative sense, the correct form is لِمَ فَعَلْتَ ذَلِكَ؟
accepted_variants: Wrong: interrogative ma drops its alif after a directly-governing preposition, so 'why' is لِمَ, not لِمَا; the retained-alif form signals a different, non-interrogative function of ma.
forbidden_answers: The forms are interchangeable: لِمَ and لِمَا both simply mean 'why', so keeping the alif makes no difference to the interrogative reading.

the retained-alif form لِمَا signals a different, non-interrogative function of ma
the correct interrogative form is لِمَ, without the alif
explanation: Alif-elision after a governing preposition is specific to the interrogative reading of ma; keeping the alif does not just look different, it points to an entirely different function of the same written letters.

concept: min fused with the interrogative ma both drops the alif of ma and assimilates min's own final nun into the mim, producing the single geminated form mimma, never a separately spelled min ma
prompt: مِمَّ خِفْتَ؟ ("what were you afraid of?") fuses مِنْ with interrogative مَا. A learner writes مِنْ مَا خِفْتَ؟, keeping the two words separate with the alif retained, reasoning that spelling the preposition and ما as two visibly separate words is safer. Evaluate this and state the correct fused form and what happens to each part.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. When the preposition مِنْ directly governs the interrogative مَا, two things happen together: the alif of مَا is dropped, and مِنْ's own final نون assimilates into the mīm of مَا, producing the single geminated form مِمَّ, not a separately spelled مِنْ مَا. The correct interrogative form is مِمَّ خِفْتَ؟, not مِنْ مَا خِفْتَ؟.
accepted_variants: Wrong: min's final nun assimilates into ma's mim and ma's alif drops together, producing the single fused form مِمَّ, not the separately spelled مِنْ مَا.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: spelling مِنْ and مَا as two separate words, مِنْ مَا خِفْتَ؟, is an equally valid and safer way to write the interrogative 'what were you afraid of'.

the result is the single geminated fused form مِمَّ
a separately spelled مِنْ مَا does not represent the correct interrogative form
explanation: The interrogative alif-elision rule is not merely optional spelling economy; here it combines with min's own final-nun assimilation to produce one obligatory fused form, and writing the two words apart misrepresents that fusion.

concept: the preposition-fused interrogative amma (an plus istifham-ma) and the unrelated particle lamma must not be conflated just because both are short function-word clusters partly spelled with ma
prompt: عَمَّ تَسْأَلُ؟ ("what are you asking about?") fuses عَنْ with interrogative مَا. Asked to write this question, a learner instead writes لَمَّا تَسْأَلُ؟, confusing عَمَّ with the unrelated particle لَمَّا because both are short function-word clusters partly built on مَا. Evaluate this and state why the two are unrelated and what the correct interrogative form is.
expected_answer: The two particles are unrelated and must not be conflated. عَمَّ is the preposition عَنْ fused with the interrogative مَا (alif dropped, nūn assimilated into the mīm), asking "about what?"; لَمَّا is an entirely different particle (temporal "when" or jazm-governing "not yet"), built on لَمْ/لام plus مَا, with no preposition عَنْ in it at all and a different meaning. The correct interrogative form is عَمَّ تَسْأَلُ؟, not لَمَّا تَسْأَلُ؟, which does not ask a question at all.
accepted_variants: Wrong: amma fuses an with interrogative ma and means 'about what'; lamma is an unrelated particle (temporal or jazm-governing) with no preposition an in it; the correct interrogative is عَمَّ تَسْأَلُ؟.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: عَمَّ and لَمَّا are simply two spellings of the same short interrogative particle and can be used interchangeably to ask 'what are you asking about'.
required_reasoning: amma fuses the preposition an with interrogative ma
lamma is an unrelated particle with a different meaning and no preposition an in it
the correct interrogative form is عَمَّ تَسْأَلُ؟
explanation: Two short function-word clusters that happen to share the letters lam-mim-alif are not automatically related; amma's identity as an-plus-ma is entirely distinct from lamma's identity as lam-plus-ma.

concept: relative and masdariyya ma keep their alif when governed by a preposition; the interrogative's alif-elision rule does not generalize to every preposition-plus-ma sequence
prompt: عَجِبْتُ مِمَّا فَعَلْتَ ("I was amazed at what you did") uses relative مَا (فَعَلْتَ has an implied gap referring back to it) after the preposition مِنْ. A learner, having just learned that interrogative مَا drops its alif after a preposition, overgeneralizes and writes عَجِبْتُ مِمَّ فَعَلْتَ, dropping the alif here too. Evaluate this and state the correct form.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. Alif-elision after a preposition (لِمَ، عَمَّ، مِمَّ) is unique to the interrogative reading of مَا. Here مَا is relative (فَعَلْتَ has an implied gap referring back to it, "that which you did"), and relative/masdariyya مَا keeps its alif when governed by a preposition: مِمَّا, not مِمَّ. Overgeneralising the interrogative's elision rule to every preposition-plus-مَا sequence produces a form that does not exist for this function.
accepted_variants: Wrong: alif-elision after a preposition is unique to interrogative ma; relative/masdariyya ma keeps its alif, so the correct form is عَجِبْتُ مِمَّا فَعَلْتَ, not the elided مِمَّ.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: any ma governed by a preposition drops its alif the same way, so مِمَّ فَعَلْتَ is just as valid as مِمَّا فَعَلْتَ here.

here ma is relative, marked by the implied gap in فعلت referring back to it
relative/masdariyya ma keeps its alif after a preposition, giving مِمَّا
explanation: A rule learned for one function of ma (the interrogative's alif-elision) must not be silently exported to a different function (relative/masdariyya) that keeps the alif; the two are governed by the same preposition but obey different spelling rules.

concept: a verb's preposition-plus-ma pairing can be a fixed lexical selection, not a free choice among semantically plausible prepositions
prompt: دَهِشْتُ مِمَّا رَأَيْتُ ("I was astonished at what I saw") pairs the verb دَهِشَ with the preposition مِنْ (giving مِمَّا once fused with relative مَا) by settled lexical convention. A learner writes دَهِشْتُ عَمَّا رَأَيْتُ, substituting عَنْ because it also seems to mean roughly "about/at" in this context. Evaluate this substitution and state the correct pairing.
expected_answer: The substitution is wrong. دَهِشَ is lexically bound to the preposition مِنْ (giving مِمَّا once fused with relative مَا), by settled convention, not by general semantic plausibility; a different preposition that seems to mean roughly the same thing in English, such as عَنْ, is still ungrammatical with this verb. The correct pairing is دَهِشْتُ مِمَّا رَأَيْتُ, not a form built on a different, semantically-plausible-but-lexically-wrong preposition.
accepted_variants: Wrong: dahisha is lexically bound to min (giving مِمَّا), not freely substitutable; a semantically similar preposition like an is still ungrammatical with this verb.
forbidden_answers: The substitution is fine: since both عن and من can loosely mean 'about/at' in English, either preposition works equally well with دهش.
required_reasoning: dahisha is lexically bound to the preposition min, not chosen by general semantic plausibility
a semantically similar preposition is still ungrammatical if it is not the verb's lexical partner
the correct pairing is دَهِشْتُ مِمَّا رَأَيْتُ
explanation: Some verb-preposition pairings in Arabic are fixed lexical facts, memorized with the verb, not derived freely from the preposition's general meaning; substituting a semantically plausible preposition still produces an ungrammatical pairing.

concept: mimma (source/origin) and fima (topic/subject-matter) are not interchangeable; swapping them changes what the clause is actually about
prompt: تَحَدَّثْنَا فِيمَا يَخُصُّ المَشْرُوعَ ("we talked about what concerns the project") uses فِيمَا (فِي, topic/subject matter) because the sentence is about a subject of discussion, not a starting point. A learner writes تَحَدَّثْنَا مِمَّا يَخُصُّ المَشْرُوعَ, substituting مِمَّا (مِنْ, source/origin) instead. Evaluate this substitution and state what each preposition actually introduces and which is correct here.
expected_answer: The substitution changes the meaning and is ungrammatical here. مِمَّا (مِنْ, source/origin) introduces a starting point ("from what"), while فِيمَا (فِي, topic) introduces the subject matter a discussion or feeling concerns ("about/in what"). Talking about a topic calls for فِيمَا, not مِمَّا; the correct form is تَحَدَّثْنَا فِيمَا يَخُصُّ المَشْرُوعَ.
accepted_variants: Wrong: mimma introduces a source/origin while fima introduces the topic/subject-matter; talking about a topic requires فِيمَا, not مِمَّا.
forbidden_answers: The substitution is fine: مِمَّا and فِيمَا are interchangeable prepositional variants of relative ma, both roughly translatable as 'about what'.
required_reasoning: mimma introduces a source or starting point
fima introduces the topic or subject matter a discussion concerns
talking about a topic requires fima, not mimma, here
explanation: Two prepositions that can both be rendered loosely in English are not interchangeable in Arabic: one names a starting point, the other names what a discussion or feeling is about, and swapping them changes the clause's actual content.

concept: ma as an interrogative operator must sit at the front of its clause to scope over the whole question; moving it elsewhere leaves the clause with no question operator in scope
prompt: مَا هَذَا؟ ("what is this?") places the interrogative مَا at the front of its clause. A learner, treating word order as flexible, writes هَذَا مَا؟, moving مَا to the end. Evaluate this reordering and state why position matters here.
expected_answer: The reordering is wrong. As an interrogative operator, مَا must sit at the front of its clause because its job is to place the whole clause under question, scoping rightward over everything that follows; moving it to the end, هَذَا مَا؟, leaves the clause with no question operator in scope at its head, and the result is not a grammatical question at all. The correct order keeps مَا first: مَا هَذَا؟
accepted_variants: Wrong: ma as a question operator must be clause-initial to scope over the whole clause; moved to clause-final position it leaves no question operator in scope, so مَا هَذَا؟ is the only correct order.
forbidden_answers: The reordering is fine: since Arabic word order is generally flexible, مَا can be placed at the end of the clause without affecting its interrogative function.

its job is to scope over the whole clause from the front
moving it to clause-final position leaves no question operator in scope
explanation: Word-order flexibility elsewhere in Arabic does not extend to a question operator's own required position; ma's interrogative scope depends on it standing at the head of its clause.

concept: ma as a relative or conditional pronoun is treated grammatically as singular masculine by default in the agreement it controls, regardless of the notional plurality of what it refers to
prompt: مَا يَنْفَعُكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ ("whatever benefits you is good for you") keeps the verb agreeing with مَا in the third-person masculine singular, يَنْفَعُ, even though "whatever benefits you" may cover many separate things. A learner pluralizes the verb to match that notional plurality, writing مَا يَنْفَعُونَكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ. Evaluate this and state the correct agreement and why.

The verb agreeing with it therefore stays third-person masculine singular, يَنْفَعُ, not the plural يَنْفَعُونَ, even though "whatever benefits you" may cover many things.

forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: since 'whatever benefits you' notionally covers many things, the agreeing verb should be pluralized to match, يَنْفَعُونَكُمْ.
required_reasoning: ma as a relative/conditional pronoun controls default singular-masculine agreement
this holds regardless of the notional plurality of what ma refers to
the correct agreement here keeps the verb singular, يَنْفَعُ
explanation: Grammatical agreement with ma is read off ma's own default singular-masculine status, not off the real-world number of the things it happens to refer to; importing notional plurality into the verb's agreement is not licensed.

concept: ma is reserved for non-rational referents and man for rational ones; using ma to ask about a person misclassifies the referent's rational status
prompt: Asking about a person's identity, a learner writes مَا هَذَا الرَّجُلُ؟, using the non-rational interrogative مَا ("what") instead of the rational مَنْ ("who"). Evaluate this and state the correct question and why the choice of interrogative matters.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. مَا is reserved for non-rational referents ("what"); asking about a person's identity requires the rational interrogative مَنْ ("who"). The correct question is مَنْ هَذَا الرَّجُلُ؟, not مَا هَذَا الرَّجُلُ؟, which misclassifies a human referent as non-rational.

concept: innama's restriction targets whichever element is mentioned last in the clause, not the first
prompt: إِنَّمَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ ("Zayd is only standing") restricts Zayd to the state named last in the clause, قَائِمٌ. A learner reads it as restricting who is standing, claiming the sentence means "only Zayd is standing, no one else", targeting the first-mentioned element زَيْدٌ instead. Evaluate this and state which element the restriction actually targets.
expected_answer: The learner has the direction backwards. In إِنَّمَا's restriction, the exclusion falls on whichever element is mentioned last, here the predicate قَائِمٌ, not the subject زَيْدٌ: the sentence excludes every other state or action from Zayd ("Zayd does nothing but stand"), not other people from standing. Reading it as excluding other people reverses which element the restriction actually targets.
accepted_variants: Backwards: innama's exclusion targets the last-mentioned element, the predicate قَائِمٌ, meaning Zayd does nothing but stand, not that only Zayd (and no one else) is standing.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: إنما always restricts the first-mentioned element, so إِنَّمَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ means only Zayd, and no one else, is standing.
required_reasoning: innama's exclusion targets whichever element is mentioned last in the clause
here that element is the predicate قَائِمٌ, not the subject زَيْدٌ
the sentence excludes other states from Zayd, not other people from standing
explanation: A restriction particle's scope direction is a fact about its own construction, not a free choice of which element seems more salient; innama specifically targets the last-mentioned element.

concept: plain inna (emphatic, full case government, no exclusion sense) and innama (restriction, ma-kaffa neutralizes the government, exclusion sense) are not interchangeable
prompt: A learner wants the restrictive "only" sense but writes إِنَّ زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ, using plain إِنَّ and leaving both terms nominative. Evaluate whether plain إِنَّ carries the restrictive sense intended, and whether the case marking here is even consistent with a reading of plain إِنَّ.
expected_answer: Neither works as intended. Plain إِنَّ is only emphatic ("indeed"); it carries no restriction/exclusion sense at all, and it governs its ism into the accusative (زَيْدًا) and its khabar into the nominative (قَائِمٌ) -- so 'إِنَّ زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ' is wrong on its own government terms (زَيْدٌ should be زَيْدًا if plain إِنَّ is meant). If the restrictive "only" sense is intended, إِنَّمَا must be used instead, and once مَا الكافة neutralizes إِنَّ's government, both terms return to plain nominative agreement: إِنَّمَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ. Plain إِنَّ and إِنَّمَا are not interchangeable: only إِنَّمَا carries the exclusion meaning, and only إِنَّ carries the case government.
accepted_variants: Neither: plain inna has no restriction sense and would require زَيْدًا accusative; the restrictive sense needs إِنَّمَا instead, whose ma-kaffa neutralizes the government, giving both terms nominative.
forbidden_answers: It works fine: إِنَّ and إِنَّمَا are simply two spellings of the same particle, both carrying the restrictive 'only' sense and the same case government.
required_reasoning: plain inna is only emphatic and carries no restriction sense
plain inna governs its ism accusative and its khabar nominative
the restrictive sense requires innama, whose ma-kaffa neutralizes that government
explanation: Plain inna and innama differ in two independent ways at once, meaning and government, and neither can be borrowed from one to patch the other: using inna's spelling with innama's meaning (or case pattern) produces an inconsistent sentence.

concept: lamma al-jazima, like lam, only ever governs a mudari' verb; the past-to-present 'not yet' meaning comes from its own government, never from pairing it with a perfect-form verb
prompt: لَمَّا الجازمة ("not yet"), like لَمْ, only ever governs a مضارع (present-form) verb; the past-to-present meaning ("has not yet ...") comes from the particle's own government, not from pairing it with a perfect-form verb. A learner, wanting to say "he has not yet gone", writes لَمَّا ذَهَبَ, pairing لَمَّا with the perfect-form verb ذَهَبَ. Evaluate this and state the correct form.
expected_answer: The learner is wrong. لَمَّا الجازمة selects a مضارع verb and supplies the past-to-present "not yet" reading through its own jussive government; it never pairs with a perfect-form verb the way a plain adverb might. The correct form uses the present-form verb under لَمَّا's government, لَمَّا يَذْهَبْ, not the perfect-form لَمَّا ذَهَبَ.
accepted_variants: Wrong: lamma al-jazima selects a mudari' verb and supplies the 'not yet' reading through its own government, so the correct form is لَمَّا يَذْهَبْ, never the perfect-form لَمَّا ذَهَبَ.
forbidden_answers: The learner is correct: since لَمَّا itself means 'not yet', it can be paired with either a perfect or a present-form verb with the same meaning, so لَمَّا ذَهَبَ is an equally valid way to say 'he has not yet gone'.
required_reasoning: lamma al-jazima, like lam, only ever governs a mudari' verb
the past-to-present 'not yet' meaning comes from its own government
the correct form is the present-form verb under its government, لَمَّا يَذْهَبْ
explanation: A particle's own tense-shifting government is not compatible with pairing it with a verb that already carries the tense it is supposed to supply; lamma al-jazima's government requires the present-form verb precisely so that the government itself can do the tense work.
